statement: Using the identity $\\sin^{2}x=\\frac{1-\\cos 2x}{2}$, show that $\\sin^{4}x=\\frac{3}{8}-\\frac{1}{2}\\cos 2x+\\frac{1}{8}\\cos 4x$. Hence evaluate $\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\sin^{4}x\\,dx$.
solution: $\\sin^{4}x=\\left(\\frac{1-\\cos 2x}{2}\\right)^{2}=\\frac{1-2\\cos 2x+\\cos^{2}2x}{4}=\\frac{1-2\\cos 2x+(1+\\cos 4x)/2}{4}=\\frac{3}{8}-\\frac{1}{2}\\cos 2x+\\frac{1}{8}\\cos 4x$. Integrating from $0$ to $\\pi/2$: the cosine terms vanish, leaving $\\frac{3}{8}\\cdot\\frac{\\pi}{2}=\\frac{3\\pi}{16}$.
hints: Replace $\\cos^{2}2x$ once more with a double-angle form.
